hops.afterHeading: How small is too small to see?
hops.title: A paper microscope that survives a stomp
hops.text: Fold some pre-cut paper parts for under ten minutes, add a tiny round lens, and you have a working microscope. Stanford researchers described this Foldscope in 2014. Bought in bulk, its parts cost less than a dollar, and it weighs less than two nickels. With a 1,450-times lens, it showed stained blood cells and bacteria. Its makers say it even survives a three-story drop or a stomp.

sources.citation: Cybulski JS, Clements J, Prakash M (2014). Foldscope: Origami-Based Paper Microscope. PLOS ONE 9(6): e98781.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A child lying on a wooden floor watches a sneaker step down beside a small folded paper microscope with a tiny round lens.
image.caption: Bought in bulk, a paper microscope's parts cost under a dollar, and its one tiny lens shows cells.

hops.title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks
hops.text: In the 1850s, many people still thought microbes popped out of clear broth all on their own. Louis Pasteur tested that by boiling broth in glass flasks with long, curving swan necks open to the air. Microbes from the air got stuck in the bend, so the broth stayed clear. Then he broke off a neck, and microbes soon grew. His experiments won a prize in 1862.

sources.citation: Parker N, Schneegurt M, Thi Tu A-H, Lister P, Forster BM (2016). Microbiology, Section 3.1: Spontaneous Generation. OpenStax.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two glass flasks on a wooden bench, one with a long curved neck and clear broth, one with a broken neck and cloudy broth.
image.caption: The curved neck trapped microbes from the air; once Pasteur broke it off, microbes grew.

hops.title: Electron microscope pictures start out gray
hops.text: Science posters are full of purple bacteria and neon-green pollen, so it is easy to think tiny things look that bright. A scanning electron microscope actually works in the dark, using a beam of electrons instead of light. It records only how strong the signal is at each spot, so its raw picture comes out in shades of gray. People add the colors afterward so the parts stand out.

sources.citation: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Small Wonders.

Parker N, Schneegurt M, Thi Tu A-H, Lister P, Forster BM (2016). Microbiology, Section 2.3: Instruments of Microscopy. OpenStax; Pirozzi NM, Hoogenboom JP, Giepmans BNG (2018). Histochemistry and Cell Biology 150: 509–520.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smiling spiky pollen grain, half gray and half being painted teal, green and gold by a person with a small paintbrush.
image.caption: Electron microscope pictures start out gray; the bright colors are added afterward.
